title: Systematic variant-to-pathway, phenotype, and precision treatment response evaluation in genetic disorders of the immune system (GDIS)
text:
Many patients with immune-mediated diseases harbor genetic variants that remain functionally uncharacterized,
leading to diagnostic ambiguity and delayed access to targeted therapies. This project aims to functionally
characterize variants in genes implicated in genetic diseases of the immune system (GDIS) using advanced
CRISPR base-editing tools in primary human immune cells. By integrating functional readouts with clinical and
population-level data, this work will accelerate diagnosis and enable the rational use of existing and novel
precision therapies across rare and common immune disorders.

title: Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core Facility
text:
Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core (B2C)
As the only Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core specializing in pancreatic cancer research in the region, the
B2C will continue to play an integral role in the Center for Diagnostic and Therapeutic Strategies in Pancreatic
Cancer (CDTSPC) and the greater North Dakota State University (NDSU) community by providing high-quality,
comprehensive study design and data analysis support to all CDTSPC and NDSU researchers. A specific
emphasis will be placed on providing this support at all stages of the research process to the Junior Investigators'
translational and pre-clinical pancreatic cancer research projects, ensuring that all projects are properly designed
and well-powered and increasing the likelihood of securing competitive federally funded research grants. In
addition, Phase II of this project will expand the B2C services beyond traditional statistical techniques of the
bench and clinical research into other emerging "big data" research areas, including bioinformatics and machine
learning.

title: Subproject 1: Compounds and Pathways for Antibacterial Combinations
text:
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections are responsible for significant morbidity and
mortality worldwide. Project 1 seeks to capitalize on discoveries about S. aureus that were made through
collaborating on innovative technological and conceptual approaches with other Project Team members. We will
elucidate two S. aureus pathways that are targets for anti-infective compounds, and identify compounds and
strategies that may allow us to exploit these pathways to treat MRSA infections.

title: Multi-modality Image Fusion to Improve Coronary Revascularization in Patients with Stable Coronary Artery Disease
text:
Coronary revascularization (CR) is a common heart procedure used to treat patients with severe
coronary artery disease. This research project aims to combine information about the heart
muscle and arteries before the CR to improve treatment decisions. It not only helps doctors make
better choices about how to perform the procedure but also introduces translational cardiology to
the students at Michigan Tech, which will connect the university's engineering research with
clinical practice.

title: Broad spectrum inhibitors of paramyxovirus envelope proteins
text:
The Paramyxoviridae family includes several pathogenic viruses that pose major threats to human health,
including human parainfluenza virus 3 (HPIV3) which causes illness or death in millions of infants and young
children, and the lethal Nipah (NiV) and Hendra (HeV) viruses that pose a risk of global emergence. We propose
to apply the results of our fundamental research to advance a potent new antiviral strategy that is based on the
use of fusion-inhibitory peptides to block viral entry.

title: Adaptive immune responses in bats
text:
Bats are reservoir hosts of many viruses that cause disease in humans. Despite their important roles in
the ecology of these viruses, virtually nothing is known about their adaptive immune responses to infection.
This project will determine transcriptomic and functional characteristics of virus-specific T cells from vaccinated
and challenged bats to close important gaps in knowledge about bat immunity that may shed light on how they
host these viruses without disease.

title: Functional characterization of schizophrenia rare variants using genetically engineered human iPSCs
text:
Recently, the Scz Exome Meta-Analysis (SCHEMA) Consortium has identified genes with ultra-rare coding
variants that each confer substantial risk for Scz, hypothesized to be in part by loss of protein expression. The
PI, Dr. Pan Li, has extensive experience with gene editing and induced pluripotent stem cells, including
development of an improved method for seamless introduction and removal of mutations, and proposes to test
the effects of these mutations in edited human iPS cells. We hypothesize that understanding the cellular
phenotypes and altered signaling pathways evoked by the SCHEMA mutations will clarify the cellular
pathogenesis of subtypes of schizophrenia, and provide potential therapeutic targets.

title: In vivo structural-based quantitative modeling of aqueous outflow dynamics in glaucomatous eyes
text:
Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness, which is primarily treated by facilitating fluid drainage to decrease
eye pressure, however, we still lack noninvasive tools to visualize and measure this mechanism in response to treatment.
This project uses high-resolution eye imaging and artificial intelligence mediated computational modeling to build detailed
3D maps of the eye’s drainage system and quantify how its structure relates to eye pressure and glaucoma damage. By
revealing new, personalized markers of disease risk and treatment response, this work will guide safer, more effective
therapies that may ultimately help prevent vision loss.

title: Contribution of Truncated TrkB Isoform in Oral Cancer Pain
text:
Pain management is a significant problem in oral cancer patients. Importantly, the mechanisms of oral
cancer pain are incompletely understood, and this impedes development of novel analgesics, We
propose a novel mechanism of oral cancer pain that will provide knowledge for future research at
developing drugs for not only pain management but also cancer treatment. Specifically, the current
application proposes to study role of truncated TrkB isoform in mediating pain at the site of tumor
development. Given that TrkB contributes to tumor progression, targeting this receptor signaling can
prove to be efficacious therapy for cancer-induced pain as well as tumor progression.

title: Identifying Vocal Tract Gestures from Audio to Reimagine Biofeedback for Childhood Speech Sound Disorder
text:
1 This research aims to improve speech therapy for children with chronic speech sound disorder
2 by creating an artificial intelligence pathway for automated, high-intensity vocal tract gesture
3 biofeedback derived from audio alone. By engineering tools that estimate child vocal tract
4 gestures from audio, classify vocal tract gesture errors to predict verbal feedback, and
5 personalize tongue visual-biofeedback displays from vocal tract gestures, this project has the
6 potential to expand use of best practice therapy in the clinic, over telepractice, and at-home.
7 This research addresses a critical public health need to improve lifelong social, educational, and
8 occupational outcomes for Americans with chronic speech sound disorders.

title: Structural basis of human cytomegalovirus replication within host cells
text:
Active cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection can manifest as chronic oral ulcerations and sialadenitis, and is a
major cause of birth defects and life-threatening conditions in immunosuppressed individuals (e.g., the elderly,
organ-transplant recipients, and people with AIDS). The atomic structures and infection mechanisms from this
project will reveal how the virus interacts with our cells to cause viral spread. The results will also uncover
novel targets for antiviral drug design and engineering strategies for vaccine design against HCMV infection.

title: Role of MAIT cells in primary biliary cholangitis.
text:
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a female-prevalent (10:1) autoimmune disease causing destruction of bile
ducts leading to end-stage liver cirrhosis. PBC is not rare, but treatments are not effective. Here we investigate
a specialized type of immune cells, MAIT cells, in causing PBC. MAIT cells are very frequent in liver, genetic
evidence indicates they are important for PBC, and they can be targeted because they are the same in everyone.
We will characterize liver MAIT cells in PBC patients and controls, and we will test genes we identified that affect
MAIT cell responses, and likely, disease. In mouse PBC models, we will analyze the effects of increases or
removing MAIT cells, and altering key genes we identified in patients, to better understand PBC and develop
new targets for clinical trials.
.

title: Computational Chemical Biology and Molecular Modeling Core
text: The Computational Chemical Biology and Molecular Modeling (CCBMM) Core specializes in macromolecular modeling of interactions, modeling and design of proteins and bound structures, hit-to- lead optimization, virtual screening and combinatorial chemistry, protein-small-molecule docking, prediction of binding sites and protein stability after mutation, computational toxicology, design of fragment-based probes, fragment growing, linking, merging, and replacement as well as preparation of presentation graphics. It has particular expertise in initial hit identification of non-traditional drug targets such as protein-protein or protein-RNA interfaces by offering high-throughput virtual screening via pocket optimization with exemplar screening at protein-protein interfaces and hotspot pharmacophore mimicry of protein-RNA interactions. The CCBMM Core provides computational services aimed toward chemical biology and translational science in biomedical research. The facility assists and trains users on computational simulations of molecular structure and phenomena. Interactive graphics and visualization tools enable users to assemble and analyze computational results. The primary interactive tool is the Schrodinger Small Molecule Drug Discovery software suite, which provides the capacity for constructing and manipulating small- and macromolecular systems, computing energies and geometries, modeling covalent and non-covalent interactions, searching conformational space, ascertaining intermolecular interactions (including pharmacophore characterization), aligning and comparing structures, computing a wide range of molecular properties, and ab initio quantum mechanics simulations. Additional drug design tools include various docking utilities (AutoDock and Dock6) and QSAR/CoMFA. Chemical informatics suites include JChem and ChemOffice, with cheminformatics analyses enabling the prioritization of hit compounds from the Infectious Disease Assay Development/High-Throughput Screening cores for subsequent SAR studies using the Synthetic Chemical Biology core. Molecular dynamics tools include NAMD, CHARMM, and GROMACS. Prediction of protein structures and protein- protein interactions are done via Alphafold.

title: Opportunistic use of existing chest CT data for frailty screening
text:
Frailty assessment in older adults is critical to guide patient-centered treatment decisions and target effective
primary and secondary frailty prevention strategies. Despite multiple frailty measures, frailty is rarely assessed
in clinical practice due limited time and resources, or unfamiliarity with screening tools. The overall objective of
this study is (1) to develop and validate a novel chest CT-based frailty screening tool with the opportunistic use
of existing chest CT data, (2) to compare the performance of this imaging-based frailty tool with validated
electronic health record-based frailty assessment in predicting healthcare utilization and death among patients
with stable ischemic heart disease and (3) pilot test the feasibility of integrating this novel tool in practice.

title: Beyond genetic heterogeneity: Disrupted proteostasis as key driver of T cell biology in age-related clonal hematopoiesis
text:
Aging-associated functional alterations of hematopoietic stem cells are driven by a myriad of complex processes
like accumulation of somatic mutations resulting in clonal outgrowth and differentiation biases (referred to as
age-related clonal hematopoiesis) and disruption of target-specific lysosomal protein degradation impacting on
activation and self-renewal capacity. We identified the interplay between mutations in epigenetic regulators and
aging-driven disruption of chaperone-mediated autophagy to mediate T lymphocyte commitment – a to date
largely understudied cell population in the context of age-related clonal hematopoiesis. Here we propose to
unravel the molecular mechanisms underlying this T cell differentiation bias and to characterize the functional
consequences of chaperone-mediated autophagy loss for T cells with clonal hematopoiesis mutations which will
deepen our understanding of diseases linked to the aging-driven heterogeneity and functional attrition of the
hematopoietic stem cell pool and the adaptive immune system.

title: Research Core (Deverman)
text: ABSTRACT — RESOURCE CORE Prion disease is a fatal, untreatable neurodegenerative disease caused by the prion protein (PrP). PrP, encoded by the chromosomal gene PRNP and expressed ubiquitously in all mammals, is not pathogenic in its native state, but causes disease when it misfolds into a "prion" capable of conformationally corrupting other PrP molecules. The goal, uniting all arms of this proposal, is to develop a single-dose, permanent PrP-lowering gene therapy to treat, prevent, or delay prion disease. Our multi-disciplinary team combines the leadership of committed patient-scientist, prion biologist and lead PI Sonia Vallabh with the cutting-edge expertise pertaining to base editing from the David Liu Group, epigenome editing from the Jonathan Weissman Lab, and delivery vector engineering and manufacturing from the Ben Deverman Lab, which will serve as the Vector Core. Cross-cutting all areas of this proposal is the need for vectors that can achieve dramatically enhanced CNS gene delivery for this whole brain disease in human patients as well as preclinical models. This need makes critical the integration of new breakthroughs in delivery vector engineering as well as expertise in vector biology, production, quality control, and characterization. Through other ongoing, fully funded projects, the Deverman lab has engineered improved delivery vectors for the CNS and established a platform for systematically identifying additional vectors with multiple traits relevant to gene therapy. This proposal will apply the top candidates from these ongoing projects to the development of a PrP-lowering gene therapy. The Vector Engineering Resource Core led by Dr. Deverman will undertake process development, production, formulation, and characterization of delivery vectors in support of the in vivo studies for all three projects in this proposal; assist with tissue handling and biodistribution analysis; develop a scalable production and analytical pipeline, and provide technology transfer and oversight for at-scale manufacturing. In the context of this overall proposal, the Resource Core will underpin the core goal of transforming prion disease therapy with a single- dose therapy, and also provide a foundational proof-of-concept for the application of engineered delivery vectors toward systemically-administered CNS gene therapy in adult human patients.

title: Using single molecule footprinting to study chromatin regulation in cardiac differentiation and diseases
text:
Gene regulation is a highly dynamic process, yet genome-wide methods that profile chromatin organization are
unable to capture these aspects. We will use single molecule multimodal footprinting to address this gap and to
resolve temporal processes.

title: Mitigating Hematologic Adverse Events in Patients with Myeloid Malignancies: A Novel Causal Artificial Intelligence Approach
text:
This study is highly relevant to public health because personalized risk prediction
and treatment optimization will reduce the hematologic disease burden among patients
with myeloid malignancies. The proposed causal machine learning methods will
effectively integrate large and multi-modal biomedical datasets for individualized
comorbidity management, which will contribute to NIH’s mission to improve disease
prevention and treatment.

title: Modeling Longitudinal Reading Comprehension in Adolescence: Protective and Risk Factors
text:
Our project entitled `Modelling Longitudinal Reading Comprehension in Adolescence: Protective and
Risk Factors' brings together multidisciplinary researchers to advance our understanding of reading
comprehension in adolescents and how reading comprehension changes over time. Our overarching goals are
to determine the structure of reading comprehension in 11th grade, clarify key predictors of reading
comprehension within and across adolescence, and to identify protective and risk factors for good and poor
reading comprehension.

title: Multi-omics Analysis of Bacteria-Host Interactions in Brugia malayi, a Medically Important Nematode with a Wolbachia Endosymbiont
text:
This research aims to unravel the intricate relationship between parasitic nematodes and their necessary
bacterial endosymbiont partners, shedding light on how these organisms interact at the molecular level. This
research has the potential to understand the molecular underpinnings of this relationship laying the
groundwork for future research aimed at targeting those mechanisms to improve human health.
